messages.content: Write a page comparing a managed database service with running your own, for a technical audience choosing between them. Around 250 words.

output:
# Managed database or run your own

The engine is the same either way. What differs is who gets paged at 3 a.m., and what you pay to not be that person.

A managed service — RDS, Cloud SQL, Neon, take your pick — resells your own operational time at a markup, usually two to four times raw compute. In exchange you stop tracking minor-version upgrades, backup verification, failover drills, and the disk filling up on a Saturday. For a team under roughly ten engineers with nobody whose job title contains "ops," that trade is almost always the right one.

Self-hosting wins on three axes:

**Cost at scale.** The markup is a rounding error at $200/month and a headcount at $20,000/month. Do the arithmetic before you assume either.

**Control.** Providers ship a menu. If you need an extension not on it, a kernel or filesystem knob, or a replication topology they don't offer, you will hit the wall and there is no way around it.

**Portability.** Proprietary layers (Aurora's storage, BigQuery's dialect) are genuinely hard to leave. Plain Postgres on your own boxes is not.

What teams underestimate about self-hosting: restore testing. Backups are easy, and everyone runs them. Restores are the thing nobody rehearses until the night they need one, and a managed provider has rehearsed theirs several thousand times.

A workable rule: start managed. Move off when a specific, named constraint forces it — a cost line you can point at, a feature you can't get, a compliance boundary. "We could run this ourselves" is true and is not a reason.
